## Problem 1

Write a function that draws birthdays for a group and checks for duplicates.
```{r}
birthday_repeated = function(n_people) {

  if (!is.numeric(n_people)) {
    stop("n_people must be numeric")
  } else if (n_people < 2) {
    stop("n_people should be 2 or more")
  }

  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_people, replace = TRUE)

  repeated = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_people

  repeated

}
```

Run it 10000 times for each group size between 2 and 50.

```{r}
birthday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    n_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(n_people, birthday_repeated)
  ) |>
  group_by(n_people) |>
  summarize(prob_repeat = mean(repeated))
```

Plot the probability as a function of group size.

```{r}
birthday_results_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_people, y = prob_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a shared birthday by group size",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of at least one shared birthday"
  )
```

```{r include = FALSE}
n_half =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(prob_repeat > 0.5) |>
  pull(n_people) |>
  min()

prob_50 =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(n_people == 50) |>
  pull(prob_repeat)
```

The probability of a shared birthday increases quickly with group size. It is close to 0 for very small groups, passes 50% at a group size of `r n_half`, and reaches about `r round(prob_50 * 100, 1)`% with 50 people. Therefore, even a moderately sized group is likely to have at least two people with the same birthday.
